opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've spent a fair amount of time thinking about, partly because it's sort of the thing I do by hand all the time, and I'd love to not have to do it anymore.

The honest answer is: they're getting better, but they're not there yet. There's a big difference between two kinds of tasks. One is the kind of thing you'd see in a research paper, where someone proposes a defense, writes it up nicely, and releases clean code. The other is the messy reality of actually breaking a real defense, where the code is a few thousand lines, written by a grad student at 3am before a deadline, with weird dependencies and half-documented preprocessing steps.

On the clean version, models can actually do reasonably well. If you hand them a simple, well-structured defense and say "here's the classifier, write an attack," they'll often produce something sensible: a PGD attack, maybe with some adaptation. On the messy, real-world version, which is what actually matters, they struggle a lot. The hard part of breaking a defense is usually not the clever math. It's understanding what the code actually does, figuring out why gradients aren't flowing, noticing that some step is non-differentiable or randomized, and working out how to get around that. That requires a lot of careful, patient debugging, and models tend to give up too early, or declare success when they haven't actually succeeded.

That last point is something I care about a lot. A model will tell you "I broke it, accuracy is now zero," and then you look, and it evaluated on the wrong thing, or it accidentally turned the defense off. So you need very careful evaluation to even know whether the model did the task. That's a big part of why I like building benchmarks here: grounding the claims in something checkable.

The other reason I think this matters goes beyond "can I automate my job." If models can automatically break defenses, that tells you something about security more broadly. Breaking adversarial example defenses is a pretty good proxy for a certain kind of security research: reading unfamiliar code, finding the one assumption that's wrong, and exploiting it. If models get good at that, they'll get good at a lot of other security tasks too, both for attackers and defenders.

So my overall assessment: the trend is pretty clearly up, faster than I would have guessed a couple of years ago. But right now, if you want a defense properly evaluated, you still want a human who knows what they're doing. I'd be surprised if that stays true for very long, though.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models doing reasonably well on clean, well-structured defenses with struggling on messy real-world code.

r002.rationale: It mentions navigating complex code and debugging, but does not clearly identify isolating the bug-relevant part from irrelevant surrounding complexity as the central difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's a mixed picture, and I think the nuance matters a lot here.

So the context is that I spent a good chunk of my career breaking adversarial example defenses by hand. Someone publishes a paper claiming their model is robust, and then I'd sit down, read the paper, figure out what assumption they were implicitly making, and write an attack that violates that assumption. Over a decade or so I did this to dozens of defenses, and the depressing finding was that almost all of them fell. Not because the authors were bad researchers, but because evaluating robustness is genuinely hard and people make the same mistakes over and over.

So the natural question is: can a language model do that job now? And the answer, as of what I've tested, is "sometimes, and more than I expected, but with a very specific shape to where it succeeds and where it fails."

Where it works is when the defense is a variant of something that's already been broken. If you give the model a defense that's essentially gradient masking with a new coat of paint, or an input transformation defense that's a cousin of things from 2018, the model will often recognize the pattern, write the right adaptive attack, and break it. And it'll do it in an hour instead of the day or two it would take me. That's real. That's genuinely useful, because most defenses that get published are variants of things that have been tried before.

Where it fails is the interesting part. The hardest defenses to break were never hard because the attack code was complicated. They were hard because you had to notice something subtle. You'd stare at the model for a while and realize, oh, the gradients are technically correct but they're numerically useless in this one region, or the defense is secretly relying on a randomness source that you can just average over. That kind of insight, the "wait, what is this thing actually doing" moment, is where I still see models struggling. They'll run the standard attack, see it fails, and then either declare the defense robust or try increasingly elaborate versions of the same wrong idea. They don't step back and ask whether the evaluation itself is broken.

And that second failure mode worries me more than the first. A model that says "I couldn't break it" is at best a weak signal and at worst actively misleading, because people will read that as evidence of robustness. The whole history of this field is that absence of a successful attack means very little unless the attacker was competent and adaptive. So if people start treating "I asked the model and it couldn't break it" as a certificate, we'll end up in a worse place than before.

The other thing I'd say is that the trajectory is steep. A couple of years ago these models could barely write a working PGD loop without bugs. Now they can reproduce a nontrivial fraction of the attacks in my old papers from a description. So I don't want to overclaim where things are, but I also don't want to be the person on the record saying this will never work, because I've been wrong about that kind of prediction before. My honest assessment is that right now they're a very good research assistant for breaking defenses, and not yet a replacement for the person who has the taste to know which defenses are actually interesting to attack and why the standard attack didn't work.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts success on familiar defense patterns with difficulty noticing subtle flaws, but does not compare performance on simplified code with performance on original real-world code.

r002.rationale: It describes difficulty recognizing subtle behavior and questioning a failed evaluation, but does not identify isolating the bug-relevant part of a complex system from irrelevant surrounding complexity as the central challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re quite good at it already, but there’s a distinction between finding a jailbreak and reliably breaking a defense that someone has put serious effort into building. If you give a model a target, let it try attacks, and give it feedback on whether those attacks worked, it can explore a lot of possibilities. It doesn’t have to succeed on every attempt. It just has to find one thing the defense missed.

The harder question is whether it can come up with a genuinely new attack when the obvious approaches stop working. That’s where I’d be more cautious. A model succeeding against a particular defense doesn’t establish that it can automatically defeat every defense.

But I also wouldn’t take a model failing to find an attack as strong evidence of security. That might just mean your attacker isn’t good enough yet. So I see automated attacks as a very useful way to discover weaknesses, but not as a certificate that a system is safe when they fail.

r001.rationale: The response discusses automated attacks and whether defenses are difficult to break, but does not compare attacks on simplified code with attacks on original real-world code.

r002.rationale: The response notes that finding new attacks is difficult, but does not identify isolating the bug-relevant part of a complex system from surrounding complexity as the central challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re already useful, but there’s a big difference between helping someone develop an attack and autonomously finding a reliable way around a defense. A model can generate lots of candidate attacks, try variations, and adapt based on feedback. That makes it a useful tool for an attacker. But succeeding against one particular defense doesn’t establish that it can break defenses generally.

The question I’d ask is: what access does the attacker have, how many attempts do they get, and what counts as success? If you let a system make a huge number of attempts and report the one that worked, that tells you something, but it’s different from reliably breaking a new defense with a small budget.

So I’d take the capability seriously without assuming the problem is solved. And from the defender’s perspective, you should be testing against adaptive attacks—attacks that actually respond to your defense—because passing a fixed set of prompts is a much weaker guarantee.
